blocks.prompt: Why the Koala Sleeps So Much
blocks.text: A koala is not a bear. It is a marsupial, which means it carries its baby in a pouch. Its closest relative is the wombat. Koalas live in the forests of eastern Australia, and they eat one thing: the leaves of gum trees, also called eucalyptus. Almost no other animal will touch those leaves. They are full of natural poisons, and most animals that ate them would get sick. The koala can handle the poison. Inside its body is a long tube called a caecum. It is over six feet long, and it is packed with tiny helpers called bacteria. The bacteria break the poison down and pull food out of the tough leaves. This takes a long time, and it does not give the koala much energy. So the koala saves every bit it has. It sits still in a fork of a branch and sleeps for up to twenty hours a day. It is not lazy. It is careful. Sleeping is how a koala pays for its dinner.

blocks.prompt: The Price of a Poison Diet
blocks.text: Every animal makes a trade. The koala's trade is one of the strangest on Earth. Koalas eat eucalyptus, the gum tree leaves that grow across eastern Australia. Those leaves are a terrible meal. They are tough as leather, low in protein, and loaded with oils and toxins that would sicken almost any other animal. That is exactly why the koala eats them. Nothing else wants them, so the koala never has to compete for food. It has an entire forest to itself. The trade is that the koala must pay for the meal. Its body carries a caecum, a fermenting tube branching off its gut, that runs more than six feet long. It is the largest caecum of any animal for its size. Billions of bacteria live inside it, slowly dismantling the toxins and squeezing what little nourishment the leaves hold. The koala's liver breaks down the rest. All of this work costs energy, and the leaves return very little. So the koala budgets. It sleeps or rests up to twenty hours a day, wedged into a fork of a branch, with a pad of extra cartilage at the base of its spine acting as a built-in cushion. Its brain is small and unusually smooth for its body, another way of spending less. Even its choosiness saves effort: of more than six hundred kinds of eucalyptus, a koala will eat from only a few dozen, and it sniffs each leaf with that big leathery nose before committing. A koala is not lazy. It is running the tightest energy budget of any animal in the forest, and sleep is the only way the numbers work.

blocks.prompt: Twenty Hours of Sleep, and the Bill That Comes With It
blocks.text: There is a myth about koalas that will not die: that they are drunk on eucalyptus oil, dozing off in a haze, and that this is why they sleep all day. It is a good story. It is also wrong, and the truth is better. Koalas are marsupials, not bears. Their nearest living relative is the wombat, a burrowing animal built like a barrel. Somewhere back along that line, the koala's ancestors made a decision that shaped everything about them: they moved into the gum trees and committed to eating eucalyptus leaves, and almost nothing else. Consider what that meal is. Eucalyptus leaves are fibrous, waxy, low in protein, and defended with terpenes and phenolic compounds that are toxic to most mammals. A tree pours poison into its leaves precisely so that animals will leave them alone. The strategy usually works. The koala walked straight through it. Its liver produces enzymes that dismantle the toxins, and its caecum, a fermentation chamber branching from the gut that stretches beyond six feet, houses bacteria that break the fiber down over days. None of this is free. Detoxifying a meal costs energy, and eucalyptus returns very little energy to begin with. The koala solves the shortfall by spending almost nothing. It rests or sleeps up to twenty hours a day. It moves slowly and rarely. Its brain is small and remarkably smooth compared with other mammals of its size, and brain tissue is metabolically expensive. A cartilage pad at the base of its spine lets it wedge into a branch fork and stay there, comfortable, for hours, doing nothing at all. Even a koala's fussiness is arithmetic. Australia has more than six hundred species of eucalyptus; a koala will feed from only a few dozen, and often prefers particular trees within those. That leathery nose is a laboratory, testing each leaf for the balance of nutrition and poison before the koala commits. The koala is not drunk and it is not lazy. It is the most disciplined accountant in the forest, and it has chosen a food no one else will fight it for. The bill for that choice, paid daily, is twenty hours of stillness.

blocks.prompt: The Koala's Bargain
blocks.text: Nothing about the koala makes sense until you understand the leaf. Start with the animal itself. A koala is not a bear, despite two centuries of people calling it one. It is a marsupial, which means its young are born barely formed and finish developing in a pouch. A newborn koala is about the size of a jellybean, blind, earless, and hairless, and it must crawl unaided from the birth canal into the pouch, which, unlike a kangaroo's, opens downward toward the mother's back legs. A ring of muscle keeps it shut so the joey does not fall out. The koala's closest living relative is the wombat, which tells you where this family came from: the ground. At some point the koala's ancestors climbed up into the gum trees and never came back down. Now the leaf. Eucalyptus is not food so much as a dare. The leaves are fibrous and waxy, poor in protein, and saturated with terpenes and phenolic compounds that are toxic to almost every mammal that tries them. This is not an accident of botany. The tree manufactures those compounds on purpose, as chemical armor, to make itself not worth eating. Nearly every animal in the forest takes the hint. The koala did not. Instead, the koala built a body around the dare. Its liver produces enzymes that break the toxins apart. Its caecum, a fermentation chamber branching off the gut, extends beyond six feet, the largest of any animal relative to its body, and inside it a population of bacteria works for days to pry nutrition out of material that barely contains any. The koala cannot digest eucalyptus by itself. Nothing can. It rents the ability from microbes, and it must hand that rental down: a joey leaving the pouch eats pap, a soft substance produced from its mother's gut, which seeds the joey's own caecum with the bacteria it will need for the rest of its life. Without that inheritance, a koala would starve in a tree full of leaves. The payoff for all this machinery is a monopoly. The koala eats a food nobody else will fight it for, and it lives in a forest that is, from its point of view, entirely empty of competitors. The cost is that the food barely pays. Detoxification burns energy; fermentation is slow; eucalyptus yields little. So the koala spends nothing it does not have to. It rests or sleeps up to twenty hours a day. Its brain is small and strikingly smooth, and nervous tissue is among the most expensive tissue a body can run. A wedge of cartilage at the base of its spine turns a branch fork into a chair. Even the fussiness is arithmetic: of more than six hundred eucalyptus species, a koala feeds from a few dozen, and it tests each leaf with that oversized nose before it commits. One popular story should be retired. Koalas are not drunk on eucalyptus oil, and they are not lazy. They are solvent. Every hour of stillness is a line item in a budget that does not balance any other way. Which is why the ending is so hard to take. The koala survived a diet designed to kill it and cannot survive us. Its habitat has been cleared for farms and suburbs; cars and dogs kill it where the forest meets the street; the 2019 and 2020 bushfires burned through a great deal of what was left; and a chlamydia epidemic spreads blindness and infertility through the surviving populations. In 2022 Australia listed the koala as endangered in Queensland, New South Wales, and the Australian Capital Territory. An animal that solved the hardest chemistry problem in the forest has no answer at all for a bulldozer.
